A_target.statement:
Assume the [[Axiom of Choice]], and for a set $X$ let $\card X$ be the least [[Definition:Ordinal|ordinal]] equinumerous with $X$.
Then $X$ and $Y$ are [[Definition:Equinumerous|equinumerous]] {{iff}} $\card X = \card Y$, so the [[Definition:Cardinal|cardinals]] are canonical representatives of the equinumerosity classes, and any two sets are comparable in size.

B_source.statement: Every set is equinumerous with some ordinal, by the [[Well-Ordering Theorem]] and the fact that every well-ordered set is order isomorphic to a unique ordinal.

substitutions.the classifying map: X -> the least ordinal equinumerous with X

object_map.reformulation: Replace each proper-class equivalence class by a canonical representative, chosen as the least ordinal in it.

validity_conditions: Ordinals are well-ordered, so the least equinumerous ordinal exists once one exists.
Without choice, Scott's trick gives set-sized representatives instead.
proof_plan: Equinumerosity is an equivalence relation, as bijections compose and invert.
By the source result, some ordinal is equinumerous with $X$; as the ordinals are well-ordered, there is a least one, $\card X$, and $X \approx \card X$.

If $X \approx Y$, the same ordinals are equinumerous with both, so $\card X = \card Y$; conversely $\card X = \card Y$ gives $X \approx \card X = \card Y \approx Y$.
So equinumerosity is the kernel of $X \mapsto \card X$.

The cardinals are ordinals, hence linearly ordered, so any two sets are comparable in size.
{{qed}}
